notes: First digest. The collector's lexical prefilter sent some off-topic Latin American Research Review humanities pieces through and held back a few relevant economics working papers; both were checked by hand this week.

flagged.why: Trade preferences: rural voters back protectionist parties and policies where local agriculture is uncompetitive, using surveys from 127 countries plus post-NAFTA variation in the US.
Multinationals and voters: links offshoring by US multinationals' foreign affiliates to incumbent vote share at the county level. US only.
Immigration and fiscal outcomes: tests whether enfranchising non-citizens changed local redistribution, using Sweden's 1975 reform and closeness of local contests.

Partisan cues: estimates in real time how an elite announcement moved partisan opinion, using minute-level survey exposure. Foreign policy, not economic, but the cue mechanism matches your trust-as-heuristic work.
Redistribution preferences: uses votes on eight state ballot initiatives to measure self-interest as revealed rather than survey-reported preferences.
Trade and migration together: explains why preferential trade agreements increasingly include worker-mobility provisions despite hostile migration politics.
Latin America and business cues: field experiment in Brazil showing legislators respond to information about an interest group's economic weight and coalition breadth.
Chile: theorizes concentrated business groups as a source of class power and dependency in the Chilean economy.

high_signal.why: APSR piece building structural-gravity measures of dyadic trade dependence that account for intermediates and substitute suppliers; likely to be used as a dataset.
Shows citizens infer party ideology from gender-inclusivity cues, observational and experimental; a heuristics paper by senior authors.
RIPE argument that the IMF's central position in balance-of-payments lending is less secure than IPE assumes as China builds alternatives.
International Organization study of how local exposure to settler actions shapes Palestinian political attitudes.
Survey experiment finding Americans distinguish less between refugees and immigrants than theory predicts; relevant framing evidence for immigration attitudes.

overview.headline: Trade politics goes local, and cues move opinion in minutes
overview.standfirst: This week's strongest work ties trade preferences to the structure of local economies, shows how fast elite and group cues travel, and links immigrant political inclusion to local taxes. Working-paper coverage was thin.

sections.head: Trade preferences follow local comparative advantage
sections.body: Two papers tie trade politics to who gains and loses inside a community. {W4414116330} uses harmonized surveys from 127 countries and finds rural voters back protectionist parties and policies where local agriculture is uncompetitive; where agriculture has a comparative advantage, the rural-urban gap is negligible, a result the authors also find in post-NAFTA variation across the US. {W7222506786} finds offshoring by US multinationals raises the incumbent's vote share in counties with more educated workers and lowers it where manufacturing and easily relocated occupations dominate. Neither covers Latin America, and neither looks at how voters learn about these effects, which is where your trade project sits.

sections.head: Dependence is measured better, and migration rides on trade deals
sections.body: {W7224848391} builds structural-gravity measures of dyadic dependence that account for intermediate goods and substitute suppliers. On those measures the world has not become steadily more interdependent, and Chinese assistance raised partners' dependence on China without a matching rise in China's dependence on them. {W7223458148}, using the MITA dataset of trade-agreement mobility provisions from 1960 to 2020, finds these provisions are driven by economic interdependence and institutional path dependence, while migration-control goals explain little.

sections.head: Cues work fast, and the messenger matters
sections.body: {W7225174171} exploits an announcement that landed mid-fieldwork: partisan divergence on military intervention appeared within minutes, before media framing spread. In Brazil, {W7224821017} finds legislators were more likely to vote with a pro-reform business group when its messages stressed membership size, economic weight and sectoral reach. In five European countries, {W7224876078} finds anti-IO rhetoric from mainstream parties lowered support for multilateral aid across the spectrum, while the same rhetoric from populist parties moved mainly their own supporters. {W7223702150} adds that voters read parties' gender inclusivity as a left-right cue. Across all four, who sends the signal carries much of the effect, which bears directly on trust in leaders as a heuristic.

sections.head: Immigration, the franchise and the tax base
sections.body: {W7113383583} studies Sweden's 1975 extension of local voting rights to non-citizens and finds a one-time rise in municipal income taxes, larger where foreign voters were a bigger share and where the previous election was close. It is an outcome-side complement to work on how fiscal concerns shape immigration attitudes. On attitudes themselves, {W7224807583} finds Americans hold different beliefs about refugees and immigrants but report no difference in warmth or policy preferences, and {W4414761356} finds coethnicity raises acceptance of Afghan refugees in Pakistan mainly among hosts who are a minority in their province.

sections.head: Latin America
sections.body: {W7224930453} develops a theory of concentrated business groups as the organizational basis of dependency in Chile, built on four major groups. {W7225245667} finds Uruguay's 2012 top-rate increase raised revenue, but income shifting toward corporate and capital tax bases limited its effect on inequality. None of this week's Latin American items is about public opinion on trade or economic policy.
